entities.summary:
The Siege of Masada was a pivotal event in the First Jewish-Roman War, marking the end of a 2-year siege by the Roman Legio XV Apollinaris. It took place from 72 to 73 CE at the fort of Masada, a rocky plateau in the Judean Desert, overlooking the Dead Sea. The siege was led by Roman Governor Lucius Flavius Silva, who deployed a system of ramps and towers to breach the walls of Masada. The defenders, led by the Zealot Eleazar ben Yair, refused to surrender and chose to take their own lives rather than be captured. The event's significance lies in its representation of the Jewish resistance against Roman occupation and the ultimate defeat of the Jewish rebels.

The siege of Masada was a culmination of a series of events that led to the First Jewish-Roman War. The war was sparked by a series of Jewish rebellions against Roman rule, which began with the Great Jewish Revolt in 66 CE. The Roman Legio XII Fulminata was deployed to quell the uprising, but it was defeated at the Battle of Beth Horon. The Roman Legio X Fretrensium was then deployed to crush the rebellion, and it was during this campaign that the siege of Masada took place. The event's outcome was a decisive Roman victory, which led to the destruction of the Second Temple in Jerusalem.

The legacy of the Siege of Masada can be seen in the impact it had on the Jewish people and the Roman Empire. The event marked the end of Jewish independence and the beginning of a period of Roman rule that lasted for centuries. The Zealot movement, which was a key factor in the rebellion, was also severely weakened. The Roman Empire, on the other hand, was able to consolidate its power and expand its territories.
